summary: The note surveys how indigenous artists in the city of New Beginnings are blending traditional practices with digital tools such as digital media, 3D printing, augmented reality, animation and streaming. It profiles individual artists and educators, and describes funding efforts like the Cultural Heritage Grant and crowdfunding. It concludes that indigenous art is thriving and that tradition and innovation together preserve and share cultural heritage.
one_line: Indigenous artists in New Beginnings combine ancient traditions with digital technology, supported by education, grants and crowdfunding, in a cultural renaissance dated September 2023.
key_facts: The note is set on September 23, 2023, in the city of New Beginnings, where a cultural renaissance of indigenous art is unfolding.
Ella Makoti, a textile weaver of the Navaru people, debuted a collection on September 12th that tells of her ancestors' migration through digital media.
Jay Silverhawk paints legends of his Ojibwe heritage and launched a virtual gallery on the first of October.
Sarah Littlecrow, a traditional dancer turned digital animator, held a workshop about how her classical dance movements give life to her animated characters.

Michael Thunder introduced an augmented reality app on November 5th that overlays indigenous art on urban landscapes; he said "Art is a dialogue, and what better way to start a conversation than by making it a part of our daily lives."
Zoe Runningwater uses 3D printing to recreate sacred totems and launched the "Totems Reimagined" series, joining other indigenous artisans in an exhibition on September 20th.
Nolan Blackfeather merges traditional flute melodies with ambient sounds and released his compositions on digital platforms on October 15th.
Rebecca White Dove, an educator and member of the Lakota tribe, spearheaded a curriculum on September 15th including beadwork storytelling for elementary schools.
Gregory Bearclaw, a documentary filmmaker of Inuit descent, launched the docu-series "Through Indigenous Eyes" on several streaming services on November 1st.

The Cultural Heritage Grant, established on September 4th, funds indigenous creative projects; philanthropist Angelina Riverstone helped set it up and said the funds are "not about charity, but investment in the cultural richness of humanity."
Jonathan Eagle Hawk's "Echoes of Our Ancestors" crowdfunding project, aiming to create a virtual museum of indigenous art, surpassed its goal within a few days of launching on October 8th.
The note argues that the essence of indigenous art lies in the cultural narratives it carries rather than the materials used, and that art is not merely surviving but thriving.
